title: From Access to Participation: Reflections from OASPA 2026
content:
Following my talk last year at the 4th Open Conference on Open Scholarship in Japan, I was thrilled to be invited to the OASPA 2026 Conference in Zagreb, Croatia, as an opening keynote speaker. The conference took place from 21 to 23 September and brought together members of the global open access community to exchange perspectives, share experiences and explore new approaches to advancing open access. The programme brought together researchers, publishers, librarians and open knowledge practitioners through keynote presentations, panel discussions, interactive sessions and opportunities for networking and exchange.

The opening keynote panel focused on the question “How does open knowledge contribute to society?”, bringing together perspectives from different areas of the open knowledge ecosystem. I joined Nataliia Sokolovska and Nokuthula (Noks) Mchunu for the discussion, moderated by Ben Johnson.

title: Beyond the Workshop: How the Electoral Integrity Seminar Opened New Doors for My Wikimedia and Media Work
content:
From 28 to 30 September 2026, I participated in the Interactive Media Seminar for Electoral Integrity at Reiz Continental Hotel in Abuja, Nigeria. The three-day programme brought together Wikimedia contributors, journalists, media executives, fact-checkers and other professionals working to promote accurate information and address misinformation and disinformation.The seminar was organised by ECOWAS and FIAP, in collaboration with FactCheckAfrica and Wikimedia User Group Nigeria, with co-funding from the European Union and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Denmark. It focused on the role of verified information in strengthening electoral integrity, promoting peaceful elections and improving public access to reliable knowledge ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections.

As a Wikimedia contributor, media professional and community organiser, I joined the programme with an interest in strengthening my fact-checking skills and understanding how Wikimedia projects could contribute to a more reliable information environment. However, what I took away from Abuja went beyond the training sessions

title: WikiMed Africa at the maiden Language Diversity Conference 2026, Accra – Ghana
content:
From 2nd-4th October 2026, I had the privilege of participating in the maiden edition of the Language Diversity Conference in Accra, Ghana, held under the theme “Strengthening Language Communities in the Open Knowledge Movement.” The conference brought together more than 120 participants representing over 82 language communities over the three days.

As a participant supported by the Wikimedia Fondation, I was particularly excited to connect with language advocates, Wikimedians, researchers, and open-knowledge enthusiasts who share a commitment to ensuring that no language community is left behind in the digital world.

For me, however, the experience was especially meaningful because I had the opportunity to share the journey of WikiMed Africa and explore how the Wikimedia movement can contribute to improving access to reliable health information in African languages.

title: Wikipedia Sent Us
content:
This story is about how the Wikipedia Community helped Wikipedian SWinxy and I go to events in New York City. As a newly re-elected WikiNYC board member, it is my responsibility to respond to my constituents’ requests.

SWinxy is one such Wikimedia community member. As the Engagement Chair, I jumped at his first request: “I want to go to this with you but tickets are $500 each.” The event was the Status Summit. I knew there had to be a better way for my photog friend to get into the event. As a Status super fan, I was also embarrassed that I hadn’t heard of the event. I emailed the organizers immediately. Then forgot. Because life.

Then SWinxy reached out to me on Discord yet again. His message seemed defeated. Confession: I am bad at checking my Wikimedia email inbox. But there it was: a code to get into the event from the helpful Summit organizing committee. We were in! And we both passed Discord messages back and forth: we were so excited at all of the possibilities. There was a countdown on Summit’s site, and we took several excited screenshots of the countdown.

Summit Day!

title: Around the Globe: Meet our Movement in ESEAP
content:
What connects a teenager in Bayombong, a 70 year-old librarian in Tokyo, and an 8 year-old student in Sabah? They all find joy and connection in contributing to Wikipedia. 

Wikipedia is built by individuals who generously contributed their time, knowledge and skills. While some came and went, others stayed for the joy of contributing and the sense of belonging felt by being part of a larger community. 

“While writing Wikipedia articles is an independent endeavor for each individual Wikipedian, it is the volunteer community around the world that has nurtured the Wikipedia ecosystem for 25 years.” 
Wadakuramon

“While writing Wikipedia articles is an independent endeavor for each individual Wikipedian, it is the volunteer community around the world that has nurtured the Wikipedia ecosystem for 25 years.”

But, in a region as diverse and geographically vast as ESEAP, the challenge is creating ways for these voices and efforts to connect & collaborate.

title: Beyond Connecting People: Building New Tools with CapX
content:
Have you ever imagined a tool that could make your everyday work as a Wikimedian easier or more effective, but eventually abandoned the idea after realizing how much work it would take to develop it?

This is more common than we might think. Building a tool involves much more than coding its features: it requires infrastructure, maintenance, and technical expertise to ensure that it can operate sustainably. This behind-the-scenes work can become a barrier to turning good ideas into solutions that benefit local and regional communities, as well as the Wikimedia Movement as a whole.

But what if you could build on existing infrastructure to bring your project to life?

That is one of the possibilities offered by the Capacity Exchange (CapX). Created by and for the Wikimedia Movement, CapX connects Wikimedians and organizations to facilitate the discovery and sharing of skills, knowledge, and experience. Beyond connecting people, its open API allows developers and initiatives to reuse its resources to create new tools and technological solutions tailored to community needs.

title: From Ubuntu Troubles to Wikimedia Contributions: A Journey of Learning and Persistence
content:
How Road to Wiki helped me move from a difficult start to contributing to Wikimedia’s Codex design system.

In December 2025, I was trying to complete the Road to Wiki selection task: install Ubuntu, set up MediaWiki, and record a walkthrough.

My laptop struggled to run Ubuntu in VirtualBox. Getting Media Wiki working was difficult, and when I tried to submit my work, the upload form rejected it. I was trying to take my first steps towards Wikimedia technical contributions, but I was already facing barriers before making a patch.

That experience stayed with me. It showed me how hardware limitations, unfamiliar tools, and a complicated setup process can make entering open source difficult. I did not know then that I would continue through the programme, work on technical contributions, and eventually see my change merged into Wikimedia’s Codex design system.

For someone new to technical contributions, the first challenge is not always writing code. Sometimes, it is getting the development environment to work, understanding unfamiliar terminology, or figuring out where to begin.

title: Wiki Bootcamp: Increasing Literacy among Small Wikipedia Editors
content:
In line with Wikipedia’s commitment to support all human languages willing to put in the work to have Wikipedia read in their languages, the Tyap Wikimedians User Group has come up with a project called the Wiki Bootcamp, which, since 2024, has been held as the Tyap Wiki Bootcamp, aimed at improving literacy among its community members willing to edit the Tyap Wikipedia, Tyap Wiktionary, and other Tyap-related projects in the Wikimedia space. As the group is an expanding multilingual group, it became necessary to experiment with a language of the community and extend the same learnings to other languages of the region with the support of the Wikimedia Foundation and other supporting partners.

The group came to the realization that if its community members are not literate in a language in which many of its projects are edited, how can they contribute correctly to such projects? Hence, the Wiki Bootcamp program, whose objectives include:

  • Boost editing: To immerse a target language Wikimedian in editing a target language’s Wikimedia project(s).
  • Language Immersion: To immerse the Wikimedian (old and new) in a target language.

title: “Ambil benih campaklah sarap”: Preserving Oral Literature Through WikiSeloka
content:
“Ambil benih campaklah sarap,” a seloko or poem in a local language from Jambi, reminds us to recognize what is valuable, preserve what is beneficial, and pass meaningful knowledge on to future generations. The saying means “Take what is good and beneficial, and discard what is not good.” In this seloko, benih (seeds) symbolizes the good and beneficial things in community life, while sarap (waste or chaff) represents things that are not good.

Oral literature carries community wisdom, experiences, and values through proverbs, expressions, stories, and traditional sayings. When these traditions remain primarily spoken, they can be difficult for wider audiences to discover.

From July to October 2026, WikiSeloka supported documentation activities focused on Jambi, Kerinci, and Bengkulu, Indonesia, making local languages and oral literature more accessible through Wikimedia projects. The project was carried out by Onyaso, Elicefa, and Fuadi Zikri, with the involvement of volunteers from Jambi, Kerinci, Bengkulu, Kaliwungu and Jakarta who organized and participated in activities across these regions.

title: How a 139-year-old family document led to my first Wikisource edit
content:
A couple of months ago, we found a bag full of documents at my house that my maternal grandmother had left behind when she passed away. Inside were baptism keepsakes, family pictures, old birth certificates, and a mysterious white envelope, among other things.

When we opened it, we found a collection of handwritten documents from the late 19th century. At first we thought they were letters, but we quickly realized they were bureaucratic papers. Through these manuscripts, my great-great-grandfather, Norverto Clavijo, was trying to obtain a promotion in the Bolivian Army. Over the course of seven handwritten pages (passed down from generation to generation and turning 139 years old in the family this year) my great-great-grandfather managed to reach the rank of commander in the Army.

The story could have ended there, but the documents also contain signatures from people who were truly important at the time. My great-great-grandfather fought in the War of the Pacific, and the manuscripts bear the signatures of heroes from that conflict. In fact, the last document is signed by the president of the Republic himself: Gregorio Pacheco.

title: Editing the Ethics of Care in Contemporary Art on Wikidata and Wikipedia: Artexte x Art & Feminism 2026 Wikiclub
content:
This year, Artexte, a library, research center, and exhibition space for contemporary art in Montreal has partnered with Art + Feminism to improve the coverage of the ethics of care in contemporary art on Wikimedia projects. The ethics of care emphasize reciprocity, interdependency, collective maintenance, and mutual support in art practices. This approach also provides an alternative perspective in contemporary art (and other sectors of society), where individual authorship and novelty are prioritized over maintenance work, such as preservation or repair.

Artists such as Mierle Laderman Ukeles have revindicated preservation, repetition, and repair as artistic practices. However, these practices often involve invisible labor that goes unseen or is undervalued, which is why focusing on care practices at the Wikiclub helps to highlight their importance in contemporary art. Care work–tasks that meet the needs of others–is also more often done by women and minorities, so highlighting it as a contribution on Wikidata and Wikipedia also helps address the gender and representation gaps on Wikimedia projects.

title: Amplifying Women’s Voice: The SheSaid Campaign in the Igbo Community
content:
The Shesaid campaign is an international campaign under the umbrella of Wiki Loves Women that focuses on the creation and improvements of entries about Women on Wikiquote. This campaign amplifies Women Voice and addresses persistent gender gap in the representation of notable women across the digital space. This year the Igbo Wikimedians User Group joins the international campaign, to address gender gap in the representation of notable women across digital platforms like Wikiquote and Wikipedia.

From 2nd September to 30th September 2026, the Igbo Wikimedia community participated in the SheSaid campaign, an initiative aimed at amplifying women’s voices and improving their representation on Wikiquote. The campaign brought contributors together to document the words, ideas, and wisdom of notable women in the Igbo language.

The campaign was organized by Akwugo, Lucy Iwuala, Sylvaline39, Ebube Clara, and Vivian Amalachukwu, who worked together to encourage participation, provide training, and support contributors throughout the campaign.

title: At Wikimedistas de Bolivia, we work with our academic idol, and this is what happened
content:
These days, writing is complex. Writing well is even more so. Through various activities and workshops, we discovered that the community of editors in Bolivia was eager to take their Wikipedia edits a step further.

If we think of it as a craft—because our work is a craft—our writing will always be something that can be refined and improved. Virginia Ayllón at the workshop for Wikipedians

If we think of it as a craft—because our work is a craft—our writing will always be something that can be refined and improved. Virginia Ayllón at the workshop for Wikipedians

As passionate editors, we often joke that having an article deleted or receiving a warning from a librarian for not following certain conventions is part of an editor’s résumé—let’s say a small bump in the road on the path to becoming a Wikipedian on the Spanish Wikipedia. Even though we try to take it in stride, we know that collaboratively creating content involves many challenges, a lot of practice, and also making mistakes and enjoying the learning process.
